title: Six days, then stop
hookLine: six days shalt thou labor, but the seventh is a sabbath (Exodus 20:9–10)

cards: A list that never ends. Answer one message and two more arrive. Clear the sink and it's full again by evening.
Work, left to itself, has no edge. So the Ten Commandments draw one: “Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God.”
Work, and then a wall across the week, the same wall for everyone. Today: six days.

teach.b: The commandment doesn't only say stop. It says labor, six days, and do all thy work. Work and rest arrive as one command, two sides of a single rhythm.
Second, notice who gets to stop. The verse keeps going: “thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.”
The rest isn't a perk for the owner. The servant stops. The cattle stop.
The outsider stops. Rest here is a kind of fairness, written into the week.
Third, the reasons. In Exodus, the reason is creation: God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh.

When the commandments are given again in Deuteronomy, the reason changes: “remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt.” People who once worked without end are told to build a week that ends.
Fourth, how it's kept. Jews who keep Shabbat mark it from Friday evening to Saturday night, with candles, a meal, and a day set apart from work.
Christians who keep Sunday call it the Lord's day, while Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. The shapes differ.
And at the end of a week, a look back: a thread on a wrist, many loves, love as a practice, then work. Where the hours go. A garden to tend and keep.
Honest sweat. And now the stop that keeps it all human.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat mark it from Friday evening to Saturday night, lighting candles and setting the day apart from work; Christians who keep Sunday call it the Lord's day, while Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday.

games.q: you run a farm with workers and animals. under the commandment, who rests on the seventh day?
o: you, your household, the servants, the animals and the stranger.
games.why: Exodus 20:10 names them all: son, daughter, servants, cattle, and the stranger within thy gates.

practice: Picture the shape of your coming week, the shifts, the deadlines, the people waiting on you, and look for an edge: not a whole day if that isn't possible, but an evening, a morning, a few hours.

Picture what you'd put down, the laptop, the phone, the list, then ask the commandment's second question: who else could stop with you? If you pray, you can hold that stopping time in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Six days. From the Ten Commandments: six days of work, then a seventh set apart, for everyone within the gates. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the sabbath, the seventh day set apart from work.
